props.title: Cutter's Way
props.initialSlug: Disabled vet hunts killer in dark '80s noir thriller

sections.content: Cutter's Way stands as one of the most haunting neo-noirs of the early 1980s, bridging the paranoid political thrillers of the 1970s like The Parallax View (1974) with the neon-soaked darkness of later 80s noir. Jeff Bridges delivers a career-defining performance as Richard Bone, a laid-back gigolo who witnesses a murder, while John Heard burns up the screen as Alex Cutter, a bitter, disabled Vietnam veteran obsessed with exposing a wealthy businessman's crimes. The film's Santa Barbara setting provides a deceptively sunny backdrop for a story steeped in post-Vietnam disillusionment and class warfare.

sections.content: Director Ivan Passer, a Czech New Wave émigré, brings European art film sensibilities to this distinctly American story, much like his contemporary Roman Polanski did with Chinatown (1974). The film's examination of power structures and corruption echoes other post-Watergate thrillers like All the President's Men (1976) and The Conversation (1974), but with a more personal, character-driven approach that makes its political themes devastatingly intimate.

The film's handling of Vietnam War trauma predates and influences later explorations like Coming Home (1978) and Born on the Fourth of July (1989). John Heard's Alex Cutter represents a different kind of veteran character - educated, articulate, and burning with class consciousness rather than just PTSD. His relationship with Bridges' Bone creates a dynamic similar to the later The Big Lebowski (1998), where a laid-back protagonist gets pulled into conspiracy by an intense friend. sections.content: Cutter's Way represents a crucial transition point between New Hollywood's political paranoia and the stylized neo-noirs of the 1980s. Its influence can be seen in later films like Against All Odds (1984) and Blood Simple (1984), which similarly mix sunny locations with dark deeds. The film's ambiguous ending and moral complexity prefigure the neo-noir renaissance of the late 1980s and early 1990s, including works like The Last Seduction (1994) and Red Rock West (1993).
